messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 76

She is a 61-year-old woman of Oceanic background who has spent most of her adult life working in security, a job she has come to value for its structure, clear rules, and the sense that she is useful and observant. Before the event that changed her life, she describes herself as steady, practical, and proud of being the kind of person others could count on in a crisis. She has lived alone for many years and has built her routines carefully around work, church, and a small circle of relatives and old friends. Her days have long been shaped by responsibility, and she has often been the one others turn to when something needs to be handled calmly.

The traumatic event happens at work and remains fixed in her mind as a moment that should have been ordinary. She is performing her duties when, in a brief lapse and a chain of unfortunate timing, she accidentally causes serious injury to another person. The injury is immediate and severe, and she is left stunned by the sight of blood, the confusion, and the sudden realization that what she has done cannot be undone. In the days that follow, she is overtaken by disbelief. She keeps replaying the exact sequence of events, searching for the moment she might have prevented it, and finding each time that the responsibility settles back onto her shoulders. She says it felt as though “everything split open” in one instant, and since then she has never fully returned to the person she was before.

At first she tries to keep going. She reports for work because that is what she has always done, but she moves through her shifts as if on autopilot. Her attention narrows; she scans constantly for danger, for mistakes, for anything that might go wrong in her hands again. Even small tasks become loaded with dread. She becomes cautious in a way that feels foreign to her, checking and rechecking locks, procedures, and instructions, and still feeling uncertain. At night, when she tries to rest, the scene comes back with intrusive force. She sees flashes of the injured person’s body, hears the sounds around her at the time, and feels the same panic rise in her chest. Sometimes she jolts awake already tense, her heart pounding, her body rigid before she is fully conscious of where she is.

As the weeks turn into months, her life shrinks around the event. She avoids talking about what happened and keeps away from people who might ask questions. She no longer wants to be around accidents on television, medical dramas, or even routine news stories involving injuries. She changes the channel quickly or leaves the room. At work, she prefers the quietest posts and becomes uneasy if anything unpredictable happens. She is ashamed of how much the memory controls her, and this shame makes her more isolated. Though she has family nearby, she keeps her distance, telling herself she does not want to burden anyone with what she carries. Her single life, once experienced as independence, now also feels like a kind of emptiness that leaves too much room for thought.

She describes a persistent sense of guilt that colors nearly every part of her day. She thinks about the person she injured and wonders whether they suffered, whether their life was permanently changed, whether they still blame her. Even when others tell her it was an accident, she cannot let go of the feeling that she should have known, should have seen, should have done more. This self-blame is not abstract; it sits in her body as heaviness in the chest and a constant knot in the stomach. She feels on edge much of the time, easily startled by sudden noise, and sometimes she reacts before she has fully understood what has happened. She notices that she is more irritable than she used to be, shorter with coworkers, quicker to withdraw when she feels overwhelmed. On difficult days, she becomes exhausted by the effort of keeping herself together and spends long stretches sitting quietly, staring ahead, as if her mind has gone somewhere else.

Over time, she has started to notice that the world feels less predictable and less safe. She no longer trusts her own competence in the way she once did, and that loss has shaken a core part of her identity. Her work as a security guard, once a source of pride, now also keeps her close to the very kinds of vigilance that feed her distress. She continues because stopping feels impossible and because routine still offers some sense of grip, but the effort it takes is immense. When she speaks about the future, she does so carefully, as though she is testing whether it is safe to imagine one.
